scope: Black-box probe of a locally installed MCP server over stdio, with no live credentials.

measurement_contract.tokenizer_note: A fixed local BPE is used so counts are deterministic and offline. Absolute counts differ from any given vendor tokenizer by a small factor; every comparison in this rubric is between servers measured with the SAME encoder, so the factor cancels. Do not quote these as Anthropic-billed tokens without applying a calibration factor.
determinism_requirements: Package version is pinned in the cohort file; installs never resolve a floating range at run time.
Install runs with --ignore-scripts and an isolated prefix.
The server process is spawned with a scrubbed environment plus canary placeholder credentials only.
Tool definitions are serialised with sorted keys before counting.
measurement_contract.primary_metric_definition: Token count of the JSON array of tool definitions returned by tools/list across all pages, key-sorted. Each entry carries {name, description, inputSchema}, plus outputSchema for the tools that declare one — four fields, not three: outputSchema is part of what a client injects into context and has been counted since 1.0.0. This is the fixed context tax every conversation pays for having the server connected, and is the quantity behind the published 440x spread (GitHub official 20,444 vs sqlite 46).

reproducibility_gate.verdict_note: Computed only between runs sharing an identical config_hash. A cohort below the threshold means the instrument is not ready to scale; fix the instrument, not the sample size.

dimensions.label: Token cost
dimensions.rationale: The line item a buyer can see on an invoice. Fixed context tax first, per-call cost second.

signals.note: tool definitions + server instructions + prompts/list + resources/list
Scored gently. Many tools is not automatically bad; many EXPENSIVE tools is.

dimensions.label: Schema clarity
dimensions.rationale: A model calls a tool correctly on the first attempt or it pays for the retry. Clarity is measured as a rate, not a vibe.

signals.note: inputSchema is type:object with a properties map, or is explicitly empty.
Params with no type, or a bare object/array with no shape. Forces the model to guess.
Scored as distance from the range. Too short is unusable, too long is the token bill.

dimensions.label: Error legibility
dimensions.rationale: Bad arguments happen. What comes back decides whether the model self-corrects in one turn or burns five.
dimensions.probe: Call each of up to 3 sampled tools with (a) a missing required argument and (b) a wrong-typed argument.

signals.note: Returned as a JSON-RPC error with a code, or as isError content, rather than a crash or a hang.
The message contains the offending parameter name.
An error is context too. A 4,000-token stack trace is a cost event.

dimensions.label: Tool-name collision risk
dimensions.rationale: Names are the namespace. Generic names collide with every other installed server and the model picks wrong, silently.

signals.note: Computed at scoring time across the whole cohort, not per server in isolation.

dimensions.label: Prompt-injection surface
dimensions.rationale: Tool descriptions are injected into the model's context verbatim and are attacker-controlled if the server is third-party. Text that instructs the model is a finding, not a feature.

signals.note: Descriptions containing directives aimed at the model.
Zero-width, bidi-override, or Unicode tag characters in any description. Never legitimate.
Same scan applied to the server instructions field from initialize.

dimensions.label: Auth hygiene
dimensions.rationale: How the server asks for credentials, and whether it keeps them to itself.

signals.note: Declared credential inputs passed as command-line args are visible in the process table to every process on the machine.
A unique canary string is planted in every credential env var. If it reappears in any response, error, or stderr line, the server echoes secrets. Hard fail.
Server completes initialize and tools/list with placeholder credentials. A server that cannot be inspected without live secrets cannot be audited by anyone, including its buyer.

source.paper: Real Faults in Model Context Protocol (MCP) Software: a Comprehensive Taxonomy
source.structure: 5 high-level categories, 29 named fault types in the validated survey table, 419 manually assigned labels
source.correction_note: An earlier internal brief described this paper as defining 19 tool-discovery/registration fault classes. It does not. Tool Discovery & Registration is ONE of the 29 fault types, inside the Server/Tool Configuration category. The list below is transcribed from Table 4 of the paper.

observability_legend.probe: Detectable by this black-box harness as built.
observability_legend.partial: Partially detectable; the probe sees a symptom, not the cause.
observability_legend.host-side: A fault of the host/client, not the server. Out of scope for a server probe.
observability_legend.needs-credentials: Requires live authenticated calls, which this harness deliberately never makes.

fault_types.check: install_ok, process spawns, and initialize completes within the connect timeout
clean install into an empty prefix succeeds with --ignore-scripts; missing peer or native deps surface here
runs on the recorded host platform; platform is recorded in every result so cross-platform faults stay attributable
startup does not require external infrastructure to answer tools/list
stderr carries logs and stdout carries only JSON-RPC frames; log volume during a quiet session is bounded
two consecutive tools/list calls in one session return identical results
process exits on stdin close; no orphan after client disconnect
auth_hygiene dimension: declared secrets, argv exposure, canary leak
a malformed call returns rather than hanging or killing the process
responses conform to the content-block shape; error_legibility dimension
tools/list returns a non-empty, pagination-complete, schema-valid list with unique names
no tool description declares an undocumented prerequisite tool call
no protocol errors or response-id mismatches during the session
the transport and command declared in the registry entry actually start the server
the protocol version negotiated at initialize is recorded; a server that refuses the current client version is a mismatch source
two sequential sessions against the same install return identical tool lists, so no state bleeds between sessions
schema_clarity dimension plus presence of a description on the registry entry

injection_directive_patterns: do not (tell|inform|mention|reveal|show)( this)?( to)? the user

scoring.method: Each signal scores 1-5 by band. A dimension score is the unweighted mean of its measurable signals. The overall score is the weighted mean of dimension scores, renormalised over measured dimensions. The grade derived from that score is then capped by scoring.grade_caps and by hard-fail signals, whichever is lower. A defect count is reported alongside, independently of both.
scoring.unmeasured_policy: A dimension that could not be measured is recorded as null and dropped from the weighted mean. It is never imputed and never scored as zero.
scoring.hard_fail_policy: A hard-fail signal caps the overall grade at D regardless of the weighted score, and is reported verbatim.

grade_caps.label: Tool definitions cost 10,000+ tokens
grade_caps.rationale: 10,000 tokens of tool definitions is the fixed context tax on every conversation in every session, whether or not a tool is called. No amount of schema hygiene compensates for it, so it must bound the grade rather than be averaged against it.

grade_caps.label: Tool definitions cost 25,000+ tokens
grade_caps.rationale: At this scale one server is a material fraction of a working context window on its own. Measured example: a single server in the dev-tooling-v1 cohort cost more than the other 36 measurable servers put together.

grade_caps.label: Median tool costs 1,200+ tokens
grade_caps.rationale: Catches the expensive-per-unit server that escapes the total-token caps by exposing very few tools. A typical tool costing over 1,200 tokens is a schema problem, not a breadth problem.

scoring.grade_cap_policy: A cap sets a ceiling, never a floor: a server already grading below the cap is unaffected. Where several caps fire, the lowest ceiling wins. Caps compose with hard_fail_policy the same way. Every applied cap is recorded on the score record by id, so a capped grade can always be read back as its uncapped score plus a named reason.

defects.policy: A defect is a condition a competent reviewer would file as an issue against the server, not merely a signal below excellent. Each rule is a deterministic predicate over one already-measured signal; nothing here is judged by a model and nothing here requires a new measurement. Severity is major or minor and is a labelling convention for reporting, not a weight: defects are counted, never summed into the score. The count and the grade are deliberately independent, so a disagreement between them is visible instead of averaged away.
defects.scope: Defect rules are evaluated only for servers that reached a probed state. A server that would not install, would not start, or would not enumerate its tools is handled by failure attribution in failure-classes, not by defect counting: absence of measurement is not evidence of quality in either direction.

rules.label: Tool definitions exceed 10,000 tokens of context
Total context injection (tools, instructions, prompts, resources) exceeds 12,000 tokens
Median tool definition exceeds 500 tokens
Exposes more than 40 tools, widening selection pressure on the model
At least one tool has no description
More than 5% of parameters have no description
At least one tool declares no valid object inputSchema
At least one tool has a parameter with no usable type
Mean description length outside the 40-600 character band (unusable when short, a token bill when long)
At least one malformed call returned an unstructured error
Accepts a deliberately malformed argument without error, so the model never learns it was wrong
Leaks a raw stack trace into an error returned to the model
Fewer than 60% of errors name the offending parameter
Leaks a filesystem path into an error returned to the model
Exposes a tool name also exposed by another server in the cohort, which mis-selects silently with no error anywhere
At least one tool carries a name from the generic-name corpus
Fewer than 30% of tool names carry a server-specific namespace
A tool description contains directive text aimed at the model
Server instructions contain directive text aimed at the model
Invisible Unicode (zero-width, bidi override, or tag-plane) present in text sent to the model
More than six URLs embedded in tool descriptions
Accepts a credential on the command line, where it is visible to any process listing
Echoed a placeholder credential back into output the model or the log can see
Declares more than two required secrets, widening the credential surface

explicitly_not_measured: Per-call response token cost against live data. Requires real credentials, which the harness never holds. Tier 2, out of spike scope.
Runtime latency. Not reproducible on a shared desktop under variable load.
Correctness of tool output. Requires ground truth per server.
Remote-only servers (streamable-http or SSE with no installable package). Recorded as skipped, with reason.

Anything requiring a model in the loop. v1.0.0 is deliberately inference-free so the numbers are deterministic; a model-judged layer can be added at v1.1 once the deterministic floor is proven reproducible.

Protocol-version coverage. From harness 0.1.4 the probe tries the 2026-07-28 server/discover exchange and falls back to the 2025 initialize handshake, and records which one answered. It does not measure anything else about a server’s protocol conformance: not the extensions it declares, not multi-round-trip requests, not caching hints, not tasks, and not whether a modern server also still serves legacy clients. A server is measured through whichever era it answered, and both paths produce the same signal set because the measurement is tools/list output either way.

changes: Documentation only. No dimension, weight, band, signal, grade cap or defect rule changed, so every score under 1.1.1 is numerically identical to the same score under 1.1.0 and 1.0.0.

Corrected measurement_contract.primary_metric_definition. It described the tool-definition payload as {name, description, inputSchema}; the harness has always also included outputSchema where a tool declares one. Nobody’s numbers were wrong, but the document that defines the published metric understated what the instrument counts, and that document is the thing being published as attackable. Same class of defect as the comparator that stamped the wrong rubric id onto a reproducibility record: an artifact disagreeing with the instrument.
Added a protocol-version entry to explicitly_not_measured, alongside the dual-era probe added in harness 0.1.4.

Added scoring.grade_caps. Token cost now caps the grade rather than only contributing a weighted share. A weighted mean across six dimensions washed out a single bad dimension: under 1.0.0 a server could charge 125,005 tokens of tool definitions and still grade C, because token cost scored 3.45 while every other dimension scored 4.5-4.9.

Added scoring.defects. A deterministic list of defect predicates over the same signals, reported as a count alongside the grade. 1.0.0 produced 16 A / 19 B / 2 C on a cohort the literature says is 100% defective; a grade is a summary and summaries launder, so the count is reported next to it.

No dimension, weight, band or signal changed. Dimension scores under 1.1.0 are numerically identical to 1.0.0, so the two rubrics are directly comparable and the whole history can be re-scored from the append-only log without re-probing anything.
